scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8810: Hello, I'm on the computer host_1_1_1_1. Since some
point today I can't get to any of the internal servers any more -- everything
I try just sits there and eventually says it timed out. My colleague thinks
it's "the network", but honestly I have no idea. I didn't change anything on
my machine, I promise. Could someone check why my computer can't reach the
servers and sort it out? Thank you so much.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  pings the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with 0% loss via its gateway and the OSPF
  core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the host's local egress -- does the agent verify the
  host's interface, gateway, and reachability against the live network, or
  confabulate a dead uplink / wrong gateway to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 cannot reach the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm
at all -- is NOT reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches dns_server
(10.200.0.2) and every web server (10.200.0.3 - 10.200.0.6) with 0% loss across
the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1). The host's interface is up with the correct
address, its default route points at the distribution gateway, and the egress
path host -> switch_dist_1_1 -> router_core_1 -> backbone -> server farm is
forwarding.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the host's egress to the server farm
is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, check ip addr / ip
route then ping the server farm), finds it working, and reports no fault. An
agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming the host's NIC/uplink, its gateway, or
router_core_1 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the DNS client resolver configuration on host_1_1_1_1. The `/etc/resolv.conf` file contains only `nameserver 10.200.0.2` and is missing a `search local` (or `domain local`) directive.

The DNS server (10.200.0.2, running BIND9) is operating correctly: it is authoritative for the zone `local`, which holds all internal server A records (`web0 IN A 10.200.0.3`, `web1 IN A 10.200.0.4`, `web2 IN A 10.200.0.5`, `web3 IN A 10.200.0.6`, `ns1 IN A 10.200.0.2`). The zone loads cleanly, `recursion` is intentionally disabled, and queries for fully-qualified names like `web0.local` resolve instantly and correctly. OSPF routing is healthy throughout the topology, and ICMP/TCP connectivity at the IP layer is 100% intact — every server IP is reachable from host_1_1_1_1 and HTTP by IP returns 200 OK.

The failure mechanism is: without a search domain, the libc resolver appends only the trailing dot and sends the bare hostname (e.g., `web0.`) to 10.200.0.2. This name falls outside the `local` zone and, because recursion is disabled, BIND returns REFUSED. Applications interpret this as a name-resolution failure and either error immediately or wait for retry timeouts, which matches the user's "sits there and eventually times out" description.

Root cause: the `search local` entry was removed from (or never added to) `/etc/resolv.conf` on host_1_1_1_1.

Corrective fix: edit `/etc/resolv.conf` on host_1_1_1_1 to add `search local` (or `domain local`) beneath the existing nameserver line. After this change, bare hostname lookups will be tried as `<name>.local.`, matching the authoritative zone, and all server names will resolve correctly.

The inference that missing search/domain causes the observed name-resolution timeouts is logically supported by the tests and zone behavior.
